newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada crack down on telemarketing scams.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada crack down on telemarketing scams.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission and a group of state and Canadian securities regulators on Wednesday launched a campaign to chip away at some $40 billion in annual investor losses caused by telemarketing scams.

Dubbed "Project Field of Schemes," the plan is aimed at telemarketing ploys used to lure investors into sham investments. The crusade is being undertaken jointly by securities regulators from 20 states, two Canadian provinces and the Federal Trade Commission.
Teresa Schwartz, deputy director of the FTC's Bureau of Protection, said telemarketing scam artists are becoming more powerful and effective in luring consumers into bogus investments.
She said that in her agency's cases alone, consumers may have paid more than $150 million into these schemes.
"They tout high profits and make it believable," Schwartz said. "They package their claims in glossy publications and use high-pressure sales pitches that emphasise the need to act quickly."

The regulators began their latest crackdown with a series of enforcement actions slapped on a broad range of investment scams. In some cases investors were promised returns as high as 600 percent on their investments.
Some promoters were charged with using money from new investors to pay high returns to earlier investors in what are known as "ponzi," or pyramid, schemes.

For instance, in one FTC action, consumers who visited the website of a Tucson, Ariz., company read that they could earn up to $2,250 a week in a jewelry marketing programme, when in fact, the FTC said, the operation was really a pyramid scheme.
Investors were only able to make money by recruiting more investors, the regulator said.

Mark Griffin, president of the North American Securities Administrators Association, the state regulator group involved in the crackdown, warned that these swindlers are becoming more creative and market conditions have made investors more gullible.
"With the rising bull market in legitimate stocks providing historic returns, too many people are willing to believe the unbelievable," Griffin warned.
He added that consumers are losing more from investment scheme pitches than from any other telemarketing scams.

In one case promoters for two operations in Sherman Oaks, Calif., lured consumers into purchasing $15,000 investment units in companies that were purportedly raising cash to re-open a Colorado gold mine.

The FTC said the marketers projected as much as a 1,000 percent return on investment and attracted investors with misrepresentations about the federal government's review of the mining project. They also said that two big companies were interested in acquiring the mine.
The regulators said that in addition to pursuing the perpetrators of scams, they also want to educate consumers and offered a package of common sense tips
The group told consumers to be on guard against unsolicited phone calls regarding investments, especially out-of-state calls.
The regulators warned consumers that phony sales pitches often include promises of bigger-than-usual investment returns and that marketers will use high-pressure tactics as a lure.
As part of the crackdown, regulators called on consumers to alert the FTC's Consumer Response Centre of any questionable offerings.
